title: RoboDyna: A Benchmark for Evaluating Robotic Manipulation under Physically Grounded Dynamics
trick: Replay the same seeded robot episodes twice, once with the simulator paused during inference and once advancing it by the measured forward-pass time, and count which episodes change outcome rather than the mean.
framing_stripped: Called a 'physics-governed, latency-aware benchmark' for dual-arm manipulation in dynamic environments with 'five capability categories', a 'two-factor difficulty design' and a 'paired synchronous and asynchronous evaluation protocol'; it is 30 SAPIEN (PhysX) tasks (20 minimal-scene tasks x 4 conditions, 10 cluttered household tasks), 3,500 scripted-expert demonstrations, three fine-tuned policies ($\pi_{0.5}$, X-VLA, FastWAM) each run on the same 900 seeded episodes under two settings of one switch (freeze the world while the policy computes, or let it run for the measured compute time), scored by binary success and a halving progress score; the headline is that the switch moves the mean success rate by at most 0.03 (Table II) while 34-85 of 700 paired episodes per policy change outcome (Fig. 7), plus a 12-person human study on the same seeds.
method_equations: Setup (sec. III-A; IV-A). A policy $\pi_{\theta}(a_{t+n} \mid o_{t:t+n}, \ell)$ maps an observation history $o$ (RGB from one head and two wrist cameras at $320 \times 240$, plus joint and gripper states) and an instruction $\ell$ to a dual-arm action chunk $a_{t+n} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times 14}$, where $H$ is the chunk length and 14 the per-step action dimension. The scene state $s(t)$ 'evolves continuously and independently of policy inference'; each episode has a success predicate $g(s_T) \in \{0, 1\}$ on the terminal simulator state $s_T$. Simulator: SAPIEN 3.0.3, $250\,\mathrm{Hz}$ ($4\,\mathrm{ms}$ physics step), each action held 15 steps, so one control interval is $60\,\mathrm{ms}$ ($16.7\,\mathrm{Hz}$); executed horizon before a new observation: $\pi_{0.5}$ all 50 predicted actions, X-VLA all 30, FastWAM the first 24 of 32 (sec. IV-B), i.e. $3.0\,\mathrm{s}$, $1.8\,\mathrm{s}$ and $1.44\,\mathrm{s}$ of scene time per chunk (my arithmetic from the text). Latency operator (sec. III-A, eq. 1). Let $\Delta_n$ be the measured wall-clock inference time of chunk $a_n$, computed from observations at time $t_n$; the execution operator $\mathcal{E}^{\delta}$ executes $a_n$ after $\delta \Delta_n$ seconds of scene evolution; $\delta = 0$ is synchronous (the simulator is paused during inference), $\delta = 1$ asynchronous. The objective is $$J(\pi_{\theta}; \delta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \mathcal{D}}\left[ g\left( s_T^{\pi_{\theta}, \delta} \right) \right],$$ where $\mathcal{D}$ is the distribution over task configurations and episode seeds and $s_T^{\pi_{\theta}, \delta}$ the terminal state under $\mathcal{E}^{\delta}$; $J(\pi_{\theta}; 0)$ and $J(\pi_{\theta}; 1)$ are the paired sync and async success rates on the same instances. Only $\delta \in \{0, 1\}$ is run. Injection (sec. IV-C): 'the wall-clock duration of each forward pass is measured, and the scene continues to evolve for the corresponding simulated duration before the predicted action chunk is executed'; 'This protocol models blocking inference and does not overlap inference with execution of the preceding chunk'. Progress score (sec. IV-C, eq. 2): $$\mathrm{PS} = b \cdot 2^{-m},$$ with $b \in [0, 1]$ a task-specific milestone value (Hit Target: $b \in \{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1\}$ by distance of the dart from the centre; Pour Beer: fill levels 55-65% / 65-75% / 75-85% give 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75, overflow 0) and $m$ the count of predefined penalty events, each halving the score. Design (sec. IV-C): 30 tasks x conditions = 90 configurations (20 conceptual tasks x {base, var1, var2, var1+2} + 10 household), 10 held-out seeds each, 900 episodes per policy per protocol, 5,400 in total; episode cap 1.2 x the longest expert episode per task; the hard var1+2 condition (200 episodes) is withheld from the 3,500 demonstrations (50 per base / var1 / var2 / household configuration, sec. IV-B). Column denominators in Table II (my arithmetic: 4 tasks per category, 'all four periodic-pattern tasks', sec. V): a category Easy cell is 40 episodes, a Medium cell (var1 + var2) 80, Household 100. Headline numbers. Mean inference time (Table II; sec. V R3): $109\,\mathrm{ms}$ ($\pi_{0.5}$), $156\,\mathrm{ms}$ (X-VLA), $236\,\mathrm{ms}$ (FastWAM), i.e. about 27, 39 and 59 physics steps or 1.8, 2.6 and 3.9 control intervals, and 3.6%, 8.7% and 16.4% of each policy's own chunk duration (my arithmetic). Overall SR / PS sync -> async (Table II): $\pi_{0.5}$ 0.19 / 0.28 -> 0.16 / 0.27; X-VLA 0.11 / 0.15 -> 0.12 / 0.18; FastWAM 0.06 / 0.11 -> 0.05 / 0.11. Flip counts (sec. V R3; Fig. 7): 'Across 700 matched task–configuration–seed pairs per policy' (the 70 non-hard configurations x 10 seeds), 85, 63 and 34 'changed outcomes' for $\pi_{0.5}$, X-VLA and FastWAM, i.e. 12.1%, 9.0% and 4.9% of 700. Writing $g_i^{\delta}$ for the outcome of seeded episode $i$ under $\delta$, the figure counts $\sum_i \mathbf{1}[g_i^{0} \neq g_i^{1}]$ (my notation); the text does not give the lost / gained split. Largest category drops sync -> async (R3; Table II): $\pi_{0.5}$ Periodic Pattern Easy 0.35 -> 0.20 ($-0.15$, 6 of 40 episodes) and State Transition Easy 0.20 -> 0.10 ($-0.10$, 4 of 40); FastWAM State Transition Easy 0.20 -> 0.05 ($-0.15$). Largest gain: X-VLA Trajectory Prediction Easy 0.18 -> 0.28 ($+0.10$, Table II; not discussed in text). Fidelity (R2; sec. IV-C): PSNR and SSIM between FastWAM's predicted and recorded head-camera frames averaged over six horizons of 4-24 control steps (0.24-1.44 s), base condition, synchronous: 29.30 dB / 0.778 overall; periodic pattern 30.33 dB / 0.784 with SR 0.00 and PS 0.06; state transition 28.69 dB / 0.774 with SR 0.20 and PS 0.31. Composition (R4; Fig. 8, pooled over both protocols): easy / medium / hard SR $\pi_{0.5}$ 0.23 / 0.18 / 0.14, X-VLA 0.16 / 0.10 / 0.09, FastWAM 0.07 / 0.06 / 0.04, retaining 56-61% of easy. Humans (sec. VI; Fig. 9): 12 participants, var1+2 for conceptual tasks and base for household, five scored attempts each; teleoperation 50.2% vs 14% for the best policy on the same conditions; scene-interactive control 77.1% ('not directly comparable to policies').
load_bearing_assumption: That the two runs of a seeded episode differ only in $\delta$, so that every changed outcome is a latency effect: 'This paired evaluation isolates the effect of inference latency on task performance' (sec. II-C). This needs (i) a policy whose action chunk is a deterministic function of the observation given the seed ($\pi_{0.5}$ and X-VLA are flow-matching policies, FastWAM samples a video; whether sampling noise is seeded is unknown (not in text)), (ii) a simulator that replays the same seed to the same states under paused and un-paused stepping, and (iii) a latency that is a fixed property of the policy rather than of the run (only a mean per policy is reported, the hardware is unknown (not in text), and in the async run each $\Delta_n$ is measured live, so two async runs need not agree either). No sync-vs-sync or async-vs-async repeat is reported, so the flip rate at $\delta = 0$ with resampled noise, the null the 85 / 63 / 34 counts should be read against, is not measured. If that null is a large fraction of 5-12%, the headline is a statement about policy and simulator variance, not about latency. Second, that the delay injected as 'the corresponding simulated duration' (sec. IV-C) stands for real deployment timing; it is blocking inference on one unnamed machine with no overlap of inference and execution, and the paper itself contrasts this with real-time action chunking [8]. Third, that the scripted and configured dynamics are physically plausible: 'We carefully configure object properties, physical parameters, and interaction mechanisms so that the resulting behaviors remain physically plausible and consistent with their real-world counterparts' (sec. III-B) is asserted, with 'A subset of scene processes (e.g. the train moving along a track) are driven by task-defined kinematic or temporal update rules', and no validation against real motion is reported.
weakest_component: The flip count has no null. 'Across 700 matched task–configuration–seed pairs per policy' Fig. 7 shows 85, 63 and 34 'changed outcomes' (sec. V R3), read as latency sensitivity, but the same experiment at $\delta = 0$ twice (or $\delta = 1$ twice) would show how many of those flips come from stochastic sampling in the policies and nondeterminism in the simulator, and it was not run; the W43 lesson (a degenerate null) applies directly. Next: (1) the stated confound, 'Because inference latency and execution horizon differ across policies, asynchronous performance reflects both action capability and execution timing' (sec. IV-B), so the 85 vs 63 vs 34 ordering is policy x horizon (3.0 s vs 1.8 s vs 1.44 s per chunk) x latency (109 vs 156 vs 236 ms) and nothing in the design separates them; (2) the flip rate is reported over all 700 pairs, most of which fail under both protocols, so it is bounded by the success count: with overall SR 0.19 / 0.11 / 0.06 the sync successes among 700 pairs are roughly 133 / 77 / 42 and the flips are roughly 0.6-0.8 of them (my arithmetic from Table II and Fig. 7, assuming the overall mean applies to the 700-pair subset; the exact base is not stated), which inverts the picture for FastWAM: fewest flips because fewest successes to lose; (3) one checkpoint per policy, ten seeds per configuration, so a category Easy cell is 40 episodes and the headline category drop of $-0.15$ is 6 episodes; no interval or repeat is given anywhere; (4) the direction of the flips (lost vs gained) and their distribution over categories exist only in Fig. 7 and are not in the text, although the mechanism offered, 'a delay can cause an action to miss an opportunity in one episode while bringing it into alignment in another' (R3), is a claim about that split; (5) the latency is one mean per policy on unstated hardware, with no per-step distribution, no $\delta$ other than 0 and 1, and no sweep that would show whether flips grow with delay (a dose-response) or appear at any nonzero delay (a determinism artifact); (6) the human comparison pools teleoperation on var1+2 against policies at 14%, where the human is time-limited by keyboard control and the policy by inference, two different latency sources that are not matched.
regime: Simulator: SAPIEN 3.0.3 with the PhysX backend, $250\,\mathrm{Hz}$ physics ($4\,\mathrm{ms}$ step), $60\,\mathrm{ms}$ control interval, fixed dual-UR5 embodiment, three RealSense D435 RGB streams at $320 \times 240$ plus joint and gripper states (sec. IV-A); GPU-batched or single-environment stepping: unknown (not in text). Policies: $\pi_{0.5}$ (chunk 50, 30k fine-tuning steps), X-VLA (chunk 30, 30k), FastWAM (executes 24 of 32, 13k), each fine-tuned on all 3,500 demonstrations and evaluated from one checkpoint (sec. IV-B); parameter counts, sampling settings and inference hardware: unknown (not in text). Tasks: 20 conceptual tasks in five categories (trajectory prediction, periodic pattern, dynamic avoidance, state transition, static-to-dynamic), each with base / var1 / var2 / var1+2, plus 10 household tasks (office and kitchen scenes with fluids, overflow, dispensing); experts are scripted controllers with simulator-state access and cuRobo planning (sec. IV-B). Scale: 90 configurations x 10 seeds = 900 episodes per policy per protocol, 5,400 in total; 700 matched non-hard pairs per policy for the flip count; episode cap 1.2 x the longest expert episode. Success band: overall SR 0.05-0.19, best single cell 0.43 ($\pi_{0.5}$, Dynamic Avoidance Medium, sync), zeros for FastWAM on periodic pattern and dynamic avoidance (Table II). Latency band: mean 109 / 156 / 236 ms, 1.8-3.9 control intervals, 3.6-16.4% of chunk duration. Humans: 12 participants with robotics background, one conceptual task per category plus 2-3 household tasks each, five scored attempts, 50.2% (teleoperation) and 77.1% (scene-interactive) on the human slice (sec. VI). Code and data: project page stated; release status of episode-level results: unknown (not in text). arXiv v1, 20 Nov 2026, cs.RO; Huawei Technologies and University of Toronto; venue not stated.
information_asymmetry: What the paired count sees and the mean does not. The mean $J(\pi; 1) - J(\pi; 0)$ is the net of episodes lost minus episodes gained; the paired count $\sum_i \mathbf{1}[g_i^{0} \neq g_i^{1}]$ is their sum. For $\pi_{0.5}$ the net is $-0.03$ (Table II, 0.19 -> 0.16) while the gross is 85 of 700 pairs (12.1%, Fig. 7); if the overall mean applies to the 700-pair base, the net is about 21 episodes, so roughly 53 lost and 32 gained (inference; the split is in Fig. 7 only, not in the text). For X-VLA the mean rises ($+0.01$) while 63 pairs (9.0%) change; for FastWAM $-0.01$ and 34 pairs (4.9%). So the aggregate hides (a) the gross turnover, (b) its direction, (c) which episodes and categories carry it (the text names Periodic Pattern and State Transition as losers for $\pi_{0.5}$, $-0.15$ and $-0.10$ on 40-episode cells, and Table II shows Trajectory Prediction Easy as a $+0.10$ gainer for X-VLA, undiscussed), and (d) the base rate: 5-12% of all pairs is 60-80% of the successes (inference, above). How latency is injected. Real wall-clock, not a chosen delay: during the asynchronous run 'the wall-clock duration of each forward pass is measured, and the scene continues to evolve for the corresponding simulated duration before the predicted action chunk is executed' (sec. IV-C); the delay is therefore stamped from the evaluation machine (unnamed) and applied as simulated time, so the run is reproducible only on that hardware and the $\Delta_n$ are measured, not controlled, with only the mean (109 / 156 / 236 ms) reported. Inference is blocking and never overlapped with the previous chunk (sec. IV-C), and only $\delta \in \{0, 1\}$ is run, so there is no dose-response of flips to delay. What is held fixed. Across the two protocols: the seed and its initial conditions, the checkpoint, the 250 Hz step, the 60 ms control interval, each policy's chunk horizon, the episode cap, the observation set. Not held fixed: the observation sequence after the first chunk (by construction, the async policy sees later states), the per-step latency (measured live), and, unknown (not in text), the sampling noise of the flow-matching and video-sampling policies, i.e. whether a sync-sync replay would reproduce itself. Across policies: chunk horizon (50 / 30 / 24 actions) and latency both vary, so the three flip counts are not a comparison of latency alone (the paper says so, sec. IV-B). What is reported. Aggregates per category x difficulty x protocol (Table II) and a changed-outcome count per policy (Fig. 7); per-episode paired outcomes are produced by the protocol but are not tabulated in the text; the project page promises 'complete results' (abstract; not fetched). Where the missing information exists. In logs the benchmark already writes: the per-episode pair $(g_i^{0}, g_i^{1})$, the per-chunk $\Delta_n$, and the simulator state at execution time; nothing new has to be simulated to split flips into lost / gained, condition them on latency, or normalise them by success count. What is missing altogether and would have to be run (inference): the null, two $\delta = 0$ runs of the same seeds, giving the flip rate from policy and simulator stochasticity that the 5-12% must beat; a $\delta$ sweep ($\delta \in \{0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4\}$) or a fixed imposed delay, which separates episodes whose outcome is a step function of timing (a window missed) from episodes that flip at any perturbation (chaotic contact, sampling noise), and which would also make the result hardware-independent; and a check of whether the per-episode progress score $\mathrm{PS}$ moves with the flip or is flat, since PS is reported but never paired. Beyond this paper (inference, L5 register): the same paired-replay-and-count instrument applies to any simulator knob that is supposed to be outcome-neutral (solver iterations, time step, contact softness): hold the seed and the policy, change the knob, count per-episode flips against a repeat-run null; the mean success rate that engine comparisons report is exactly the quantity this paper shows to be insensitive.
occupies: Published: a 30-task SAPIEN / PhysX dual-arm benchmark (20 conceptual tasks in five dynamic-capability categories with base / var1 / var2 / var1+2 conditions, 10 household tasks), 3,500 scripted-expert demonstrations with the var1+2 condition withheld, the execution operator $\mathcal{E}^{\delta}$ with $\delta \in \{0, 1\}$ as a paired synchronous / asynchronous protocol on identical seeds where the asynchronous arm advances the scene by the measured wall-clock forward-pass time, the progress score $\mathrm{PS} = b \cdot 2^{-m}$, success rates below 0.20 for $\pi_{0.5}$, X-VLA and FastWAM over 5,400 episodes, mean sync-async success differences of at most 0.03 against 85 / 63 / 34 changed outcomes per 700 matched pairs, the observation that FastWAM's PSNR / SSIM is not monotone with its success across categories and that it never succeeds on tasks whose dynamics it mispredicts, 56-61% retention on the held-out composition, and a 12-participant human baseline (50.2% teleoperation, 77.1% scene-interactive) on the same seeds.

theme_fit.why: scout_theme 'eval latency validity': the headline a stranger would repeat is that letting the simulator run while the policy thinks flips 5-12% of episode outcomes (85 / 63 / 34 of 700 matched pairs) while the mean success rate moves at most 0.03, so frozen-world synchronous evaluation and the mean success rate are both blind to latency; measurement register, solo-probeable (the benchmark, seeds and three checkpoints exist), not a frontier recipe fight

the simulator advances while the policy thinks is a protocol-validity question about simulated evaluation, and the paired-seed replay-and-count instrument is the per-episode audit the lane wants, applied here to one knob (pause vs advance) instead of iteration caps or time steps; SAPIEN / PhysX single-environment, not a GPU-batched engine, and no physics is verified, so it supplies an instrument and a neighbour, not an answer to the lane sentence

outcome-level flips hidden by averages is benchmark validity and attribution of outcome variance (latency vs policy vs simulator noise), with the missing null (sync-sync repeat) as the attribution gap; robot policies rather than LLM agents, and only three policies, one checkpoint each, ten seeds per configuration

inference latency is costed in task outcomes (109-236 ms per chunk against 60 ms control intervals), the first time the lane's cost-of-compute concern appears as a benchmark switch; but no serving, batching or hardware measurement is made and the hardware is unnamed

limitations_as_complaints: My asynchronous protocol stops the policy from acting while it thinks and never lets the next chunk's inference overlap the current chunk's execution, so the latency penalty I measure is the worst case and the deployment regime every real-time controller actually uses is outside my benchmark: 'This protocol models blocking inference and does not overlap inference with execution of the preceding chunk, as in real-time action chunking' (sec. IV-C, Evaluation Protocols).

My three policies differ in both how long they think (109 / 156 / 236 ms) and how many actions they execute before looking again (50 / 30 / 24), so when their flip counts differ (85 / 63 / 34 of 700) I cannot say whether latency or horizon did it: 'Because inference latency and execution horizon differ across policies, asynchronous performance reflects both action capability and execution timing' (sec. IV-B, Training).

My world-model fidelity ruler is a whole-frame PSNR / SSIM that stays high when the one moving object is wrong, so it cannot tell me whether the model predicted the thing the task depends on, which is why fidelity and success disagree across my categories: 'Because these metrics are computed over the full frame, they are dominated by static background pixels, hence can remain high even when a small moving object is mispredicted' (sec. V, R2).
